title: Everything is quantum, including you
subtitle: In conversation with Vlatko Vedral
author: Vlatko Vedral
introduction: We never see tables in two places at once or cats that are both dead and alive—yet this is exactly what quantum mechanics predicts. As a result, it has typically been assumed that quantum mechanics only applies to small scales. But according to Oxford physicist Vlatko Vedral, this is a radical mistake. The universe is quantum at every scale, and we only get paradoxes of quantum mechanics when we insist on a classical world outside it. In this interview, IAI contributing editor Ozbir Kip challenges Vedral on whether reality is really quantum all the way up.
body:
Kip: Your work is primarily in quantum information. Most of us are familiar with or have heard of quantum mechanics. Can you tell us a bit about what quantum information is as a field of study?

Vedral: Yes, this was a big revolution that started maybe in the ‘60s and ‘70s. It was a realization that how much information you can encode into a physical system and how quickly you can process this information are not abstract mathematical laws, but fundamentally depend on the laws of physics.

That was a huge step because in the ‘60s and ‘70s, various researchers realized that the laws of classical physics are not sufficient if you’re ultimately going to encode information into quantum systems. And even more excitingly, not only does classical physics fail; actually, quantum mechanics allows you to do better. You can store more information and you can process it much faster. And that’s really the field of quantum information.

You start your book by talking about the different interpretations of quantum mechanics, and you don’t think any of them succeed. Why is that?

Yes, I think that’s extremely interesting as a question, which is not obvious at all: how what we call the Copenhagen interpretation really became the dominant interpretation of quantum mechanics. The name comes from the fact that Niels Bohr, the Danish physicist, one of the pioneers of quantum physics, really was promoting it in the mid-’20s, right when quantum mechanics was discovered. He had a number of people in his group—Heisenberg was there, Pauli was there—and a number of other luminaries, who I think agreed more or less with Bohr that this was the way to think about it.

SUGGESTED READING 100 years of quantum mechanics: a new approach is needed By Emily Adlam

There were a number of other possibilities there. Some people advocated that maybe there will be a return to physics that looks more like classical physics—that there would be some kind of hidden variables that we may be able to find that go beyond quantum mechanics and actually turn it back into a form of classical physics. And we have a lot of other interpretations.

I think the closest to reality, in my view, is what is known as the many-worlds interpretation. I object more to the name of this interpretation than what it says. I think the details are correct—maybe not all the details. In the Copenhagen interpretation, people advocate that in order to understand the quantum realm, we always need an outside classical domain. And that’s what I’m arguing against in my book. The argument in the book is really that no hybrid account—a universe which is half classical and half quantum—will really be able to capture all of the phenomena that we are aware of. It’s ultimately inconsistent in my view.

This is certainly the problem with hidden variables as well, because they’re advocating that there is classicality even within quantum mechanics. So that’s even more classical than anything else. Many-worlds takes the idea seriously that the universe is quantum through and through, but it talks about many universes existing in parallel. And I think what I would argue instead is that we are talking about a single universe, but that everything in this universe has quantum mechanical properties.

Can you tell us what Q numbers are? They feature a lot in your book, and you distinguish them from C numbers. What is the distinction?

C, of course, stands for classical numbers and Q stands for quantum numbers (that’s Dirac’s language). The idea is that the classical numbers are simply what we are used to in classical physics, the real numbers that describe properties of classical logic. So if you say the velocity of an object is 10 meters per second, then this 10 is simply your C number that pertains to the property, one of the possible properties of your system.

What happened that triggered the whole revolution in 1925 was Heisenberg’s idea. That’s the first paper that marks the beginning of quantum mechanics. What Heisenberg said is that the dynamical laws of classical physics are actually fine. It’s not that we need to change the dynamics of these objects. So, for instance, Newton’s dynamical laws are perfectly fine. Maxwell’s equations for light are also fine according to Heisenberg, but the entities that obey these equations—so when you talk about acceleration or a mass or a force or anything else, electric and magnetic fields—classically, these are just simple real numbers. They are the C numbers that Dirac was talking about. Heisenberg said: we are going to get the right behavior and we’re going to match it perfectly with experiments if we substitute these classical numbers with more complicated entities.

No hybrid account—a universe which is half classical and half quantum—will really be able to capture all of the phenomena that we are aware of.

Incidentally, it’s very interesting that he didn’t know what these entities were. He thought that he was introducing them mathematically. He was basically using tables of elements, which we call matrices, and they were known at that time. They were maybe not the standard part of a physics curriculum, but certainly many physicists were aware of matrices. He wasn’t; he literally invented matrices independently. These are tables of numbers that are frequently infinitely big. So in order to talk about a position or a speed of your particle, you can’t just get away with a single number as we do in Newtonian physics, but you need to introduce infinitely many numbers to characterize each of these properties.

And Heisenberg said, if you do that, you can then solve the same old equations. You don’t need to change the equations and you will get the correct behavior. And this was ingenious, and it really does work.

Interesting. And then I suppose Schrödinger comes along and sort of alters this picture so that everything is a wave. So how do you see that transition?

Indeed. That’s exactly what I combined in my picture. And I think this combination allows us to retain Q numbers, i.e. the waves, even from classical physics with the modification introduced by Q numbers, and also then end up talking about a single universe in which everything behaves as a quantum wave.

Schrödinger had a completely different approach. I think he really wanted to depart much less from classical physics. He loved the idea of de Broglie. De Broglie was the person who suggested that everything, even electrons, even particles that we traditionally think behave like particles, should actually behave like waves. That’s very interesting because what that implies is that an electron, when there are no forces acting on it, would go in a straight line according to Newton. But according to quantum mechanics, it actually diffuses much like a wave would. And so that was the suggestion of de Broglie. But de Broglie didn’t have a wave equation that would describe that behavior.

Schrödinger was then the person who, once he had the idea, understood what de Broglie was talking about. He actually sat down and wrote what we now call the Schrödinger equation. In classical physics, we have particles which behave very differently to waves. They are completely different entities. They obey different theories, Newton’s theory and Maxwell’s equations, whereas with Schrödinger’s discovery, suddenly everything becomes a wave.

But of course, we shouldn’t think of these waves as classical waves. If you think of them as classical waves, we are back to kind of hidden variables, and we know that that doesn’t work—it is contradicted by our experiments. So it’s not enough that they are waves. What must happen is that the key properties of these waves, for instance, the height of the wave, if you’re talking about the amplitude of the wave, and that’s the thing that changes in time as the wave propagates, that amplitude is no longer a C number in quantum mechanics. It must actually become one of these Q numbers. This happens to be an infinity times infinity matrix, according to Heisenberg. And if you put that together with Schrödinger’s idea, I think that’s the best picture of reality that we have at present.

We think of quantum mechanics as applying at the microscopic scale. Einstein and Bohr thought that too. But you advocate the view that it also applies to macroscopic objects like tables, chairs, humans, and so on. How can we make sense of this view? Why don’t we see trees, for example, exhibiting quantum behavior?

Yes, that’s a very profound question. Indeed, as I said in the book, there are many interpretations, and we still argue about it in the research community. So certainly the question is not at all settled. What prompted me to write about the experiments that I write about in the book is precisely that we should be more ambitious and really try to test some of these aspects. Of course, I have my own view on this, but I’m perfectly prepared, like any other physicist is, to be contradicted by some of these experiments. And I think that would be hugely important for us. It would signal probably the end of quantum mechanics, or even general relativity, and the beginning of something else.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The future of entanglement With Tim Maudlin, Ivette Fuentes, Jacob Barandes

What’s interesting in the question you ask—“why don’t we see superpositions all around us?”—is that quantum mechanics, in my view, explains even that, and that’s what’s interesting about it. But I think it only explains that if you assume that everything is quantum mechanical, as I’m advocating. So whenever you hear that there is an apparent paradox in quantum mechanics (the EPR paradox, the Schrödinger’s cat paradox, the double slit experiment, etc.), I think they are only considered paradoxical by people who do not view everything as quantum mechanical in the universe.

Let me answer your question more specifically. What seems to be happening when we make an observation is that the Q numbers that pertain to us—when I say us, I’m including all other bits of equipment that are relevant, including microscopes we use to amplify microscopic phenomena—couple to the Q numbers of another system, and we get an entangled state. It’s this entanglement that leads to effectively classical realities, specifically a multitude of them, which the Q numbers would suggest all exist simultaneously. However, they are exactly correlated in a way that, in one of these classical realities, only two numbers are correlated from the quantum numbers that engage in the interaction. In another reality, there will be two different numbers correlated, and so on.

So, for instance, if you have a superposition of an object in two places at the same time, when you measure the object, you will never see it in two places at the same time. And what I’m advocating is that this is a direct consequence of quantum mechanics. This is not something we need to add to the quantum formalism. It’s simply a consequence of the fact that our Q numbers, if you like, part of our perception and the apparatus and everything else, become entangled with the Q numbers of this particle. And it’s that entanglement that leads us to see single individual outcomes. So it’s very subtle in a sense how the macroscopic reality that we see, which you rightly point out looks extremely classical to us (we are not directly aware of any of these quantum phenomena), is actually still a consequence of a fully quantum mechanical universe.

A large part of your book is devoted to quantum gravity. Almost every physicist working in this field is a theoretician, and doesn’t really care whether their theory is testable or not. How important is it to you that our theory of quantum gravity be testable?

Extremely. I think otherwise it’s really a branch of philosophy. The only arguments that you can use in theory are certain consistency arguments. For instance, you can say if you quantize gravity that way you might be violating some principle or other, let’s say energy conservation. That’s why I think, for instance, that many of these semi-classical approaches, in which gravity is left classical, and the rest of the world is quantum mechanical, suffer from all sorts of inconsistencies.

However, as we saw with the EPR paradox and everything else, there is nothing to suggest that nature agrees with my point of view or with whatever we physicists consider to be consistent. Maybe nature will surprise us in this respect as well. No matter how tight your argument looks logically or mathematically, we know historically that we’ve been surprised by experiment many times. I think it’s crucial that we perform these experiments.

You can no longer sit under a tree and just think about it axiomatically as Euclid might have done.

Needless to say, and I think I’m very open about it in my own book, I actually think that quantum mechanics will survive at that level and that we will discover that certain elements of the gravitational field which are relevant for this low-energy regime must ultimately become quantum mechanical. But secretly, I must admit, I’m actually hoping that this fails because it would be a much bigger surprise and would really then force us to radically rethink the foundations of even the Standard Model, our best description that we have at present. So in a way, I think logic and consistency would tell me that gravity ought to be quantized. That seems to be the most logical way to proceed. However, nature may disagree with this. And I think that would really be much more interesting for us physicists because it would force us to think even harder about that.

I want to talk a little about the philosophy behind your view. Near the end of your book, you have a discussion on whether mathematics constrains physics or vice versa, and I suppose you defend the latter view. Why do you believe it must be this way round?

This, as you said, is part of philosophy. These ideas go back to the ancient Greeks. And I think we’ve been discussing them for over two and a half millennia. And I don’t think anyone really has a conclusive answer. Obviously, these are not things that you can really experiment with in the way that we can do so in physics to eliminate various hypotheses.

Euclid wrote the Elements, completely axiomatically, and those are basically the axioms that we, more or less with slight modifications, use even now. So I think Euclid thought about it in a very abstract way, as mathematicians tend to think.

But with the discovery of general relativity, the converse idea received a considerable boost, because Einstein said that the kind of geometry we live in is not an abstract mathematical question, but that you really have to go out there in the universe. For instance, you have to measure the angles in various triangles and you have to see whether they add up to 180 degrees, which they would in flat geometry. However, if the geometry of the universe is not flat, then you could either get more than 180 degrees or less than 180 degrees, depending on what kind of universe we live in. So suddenly the question of geometry became a question of experimental physics and not of abstract mathematics. You can no longer sit under a tree and just think about it axiomatically as Euclid might have done, but you have to engage in exactly the same practices as we do in physics.

And then the second time that this happened, which was even more significant for me, was exactly how we started our discussion: quantum information. The laws of information and computation are not really abstract mathematical laws, even though the people who pioneered these approaches, like Claude Shannon and Alan Turing, thought about computation and information completely independently of the laws of physics. They were not physicists; they were probably not even familiar with quantum mechanics at the time when they were developing their ideas—very much like the ancient Greeks and geometry. And then suddenly, a couple of decades later, people came along and said our laws of information are no longer correct, so we have to modify them in light of what quantum systems can do. If you want to understand how much information we can encode and how quickly we can process it, you really have to understand the underlying laws of physics. That’s what dictates this.

So in my book, I’m trying to be playful and to expand on this idea to say that maybe even the rest of mathematics, maybe even number theory, the fact that we have integers, for instance, is really just a consequence of quantum mechanics. It looks like a beautiful possibility to me.

Vlatko, thank you very much for this conversation.

Vlatko Vedral's new book,Portals to a New Reality: Five Experiments to Unlock the Future of Physics, is publishedby Penguinon the 29th October.
